title: Not everything is kamma
hook: asked whether all feeling comes from past deeds, the Buddha says no: weather, illness and more play a part (SN 36.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday: as you sow, and your line was the same. Did you plant one good seed, and manage not to keep checking on it? Day three hundred seventy-four.

Someone you love gets sick. And sooner or later, someone says it, kindly or not: it must be their karma. Maybe something from a past life. Sometimes the sick person says it about themselves, lying awake at three in the morning: what did I do to deserve this? It's one of the most common things people assume Buddhism teaches. The Buddha was asked about it directly, by a wandering ascetic named Sivaka, and his answer surprises nearly everyone who hears it. Today: not everything is kamma.
screen: `IT MUST BE THEIR KARMA.` → `WHAT DID I DO TO DESERVE THIS?` → `SIVAKA ASKS.`

segments.voice: Sivaka puts it plainly. Some teachers say that whatever a person feels, pleasant, painful or neither, is all caused by what they did in the past. What do you say? The Buddha says no, and gives a list. Some feelings, Sivaka, arise from bile. Some from phlegm. Some from wind, which in the medicine of his day meant the body's inner airs. Some from a mix of these. Some from a change of season, the weather. Some from careless behavior, how a person treats their own body. Some from assault, what someone else does to you. And some from the ripening of kamma. Eight causes. Kamma is one of them. Then he says something sharp about the teachers who claim it's all past deeds. They go beyond what a person can know for themselves, and beyond what the world agrees is true. Anyone can see that a cold snap brings on aches. So kamma is real in this teaching, and it isn't the whole explanation. Later Buddhist thinkers worked out in detail how kamma and other conditions weave together, and they don't all draw the lines in the same place. But the sutta's practical point is hard to miss. Telling a sick person their illness is their own doing isn't wisdom by this text. It claims to know what no one in the room can know. The response that fits the sutta is the one a good doctor and a good friend would give anyway: let's look after you.
screen: `SIVAKA'S QUESTION.` · `EIGHT CAUSES, KAMMA IS ONE.` · `BEYOND WHAT ANYONE CAN KNOW.` · `LET'S LOOK AFTER YOU.` · then, large: `NOT EVERYTHING IS KAMMA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind someone who is unwell or struggling right now; it may be you. Notice whether any blaming thought is hiding in the picture: they should have, I should have, it's because. Don't argue with it. Just set it gently to one side, the way you'd move a coat off a chair so someone can sit down. Then let what's left be simple care, the plain wish that they're looked after. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Not everything is kamma. In the Connected Discourses the Buddha names eight causes of feeling, from bile to weather to assault, and kamma is only one.
Your line: not everything is kamma. Today, refuse to blame a sick person, including yourself, and offer care instead. Day three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities visit and care for the sick, and monks are traditionally invited to chant protective verses for the ill; teachers often cite this sutta to correct the idea that illness is simply a punishment.

fork.setup: your friend's mother is seriously ill. someone at the hospital says, "it's her karma." by SN 36.21, what's the fair reply?
options: agree; all feeling comes from past deeds.
no one can know that; kamma is one cause among many.
say it's the family's karma instead.
fork.reveal: the Buddha tells Sivaka that claiming all feeling comes from past kamma oversteps what anyone can know; bodily causes, weather, carelessness and assault count too.

original.note: Pali vedanā: feeling, pleasant, painful or neither. SN 36.21 asks where it comes from.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Buddhism, whatever happens to you is your karma.
what it means: kamma is one cause among eight in this sutta; the body, the weather, carelessness and other people count too.
what a scholar hears: the list's bile, phlegm and wind match the three humors of early Indian medicine, and the Milindapañha later cites the same list to argue that not all suffering is kamma.

sources.ref: Milindapañha (the questions of King Milinda, on whether all feeling is kamma)

notes: SN 36.21 paraphrased; the eight causes (bile, phlegm, wind, their combination, change of climate, careless behavior, assault, kamma-result) and the 'overshoot what is known by oneself and by the world' remark. Confirm.
Milindapañha reference (Book IV, the Buddha's illness/Devadatta's rock dilemma) cites this list; confirm location.
'Later Buddhist thinkers... don't all draw the lines in the same place': deliberately general; some teachers hold kamma conditions even 'other' causes indirectly.
Equation of bile/phlegm/wind with early Indian medical humors is standard but should be checked.
